Abstract.

Preorder polytopes, defined from preorders on finite sets, are introduced and studied from a lattice point enumeration point of view. They naturally generalize arbor polytopes, recently introduced and studied by the second named author. Preorder polytopes are shown to be lattice polytopes which satisfy a certain duality relating their Ehrhart polynomials with the zeta polynomials of their posets of lattice points. A combinatorial interpretation of the normalized volume of a preorder polytope is proven, together with formulas for the Ehrhart polynomial and the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial, and a combinatorial interpretation of the latter is conjectured. Several conjectures and results on the lattice point enumeration of arbor polytopes are generalized to preorder polytopes, new conjectures are proposed and new interesting examples of preorder polytopes are studied.

1. Introduction

Arbor polytopes are lattice polytopes introduced and studied in [Cha25b]. This paper studies a natural generalization. Let us first recall the definition and main properties of arbor polytopes. Given a finite set EE, an arbor on EE is a rooted tree with vertices the blocks of a partition of EE. The arbor polytope associated to such an arbor σ\sigma is the polytope 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} in ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E} defined by the linear inequalities xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0 for e∈Ee\in E and

(1) ∑e∈𝒟⁡(v)xe≤|𝒟⁡(v)|\sum_{e\in\mathscr{D}(v)}x_{e}\leq|\mathscr{D}(v)|

for every vertex vv of σ\sigma, where 𝒟⁡(v)\mathscr{D}(v) is the union of all vertices which are descendants of vv in σ\sigma (including vv itself). The set of lattice points of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma}, denoted by PσP_{\sigma} and partially ordered as a subposet of the product order ℕE\mathbb{N}^{E}, also plays a central role in [Cha25b]. It was shown there that 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} is a simple lattice polytope with very interesting properties from a lattice point enumeration point of view.

Let us present two conjectures and one result about arbor polytopes which partly motivated the present work (see Section 2 for relevant background and any undefined terminology). Let us denote by hi​(σ)h_{i}(\sigma) the number of lattice points of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} having ii nonzero coordinates for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n and set h⁡(σ,t)=∑i=0nhi​(σ)​tih(\sigma,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}h_{i}(\sigma)t^{i}, where nn is the cardinality of the ground set EE. Following [Cha25b], we call h⁡(σ,t)h(\sigma,t) the hh-polynomial of σ\sigma.

Conjecture 1.1.

([Cha25b, Conjecture 1.1]) The polynomial h⁡(σ,t)h(\sigma,t) is equal to the hh-polynomial of an nn-dimensional simplicial polytope for every arbor σ\sigma on an nn-element set EE. In particular, h⁡(σ,t)h(\sigma,t) is palindromic and unimodal.

Conjecture 1.2.

([Cha25b, Conjecture 3.2]) For every arbor σ\sigma, all roots of the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} are real and lie in the interval [−1,0][-1,0]. In particular, the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} has only real roots.

An arbor σ\sigma is said to be linear if the associated rooted tree is a path. The reverse arbor rev⁡(σ){\rm rev}(\sigma) is then defined by reversing the order of the vertices of this path. The following statement was conjectured in [Cha25b, Section 4].

Theorem 1.3.

([Ath25, Theorem 1.3]) The Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} and the zeta polynomial of Prev⁡(σ)P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)} are related by the identity

Ehr⁡(𝒬σ,t)=𝒵⁡(Prev⁡(σ),t+1){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma},t)={\mathcal{Z}}(P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)},t+1)

for every linear arbor σ\sigma.

This paper generalizes arbor polytopes by replacing arbors on finite sets by arbitrary preorders. A preorder on a finite set EE can be viewed as a partial order on the set of blocks of a partition of EE, called vertices (see Section 2.2). The example shown in Figure 1 will serve as a running example. Given a preorder τ\tau on a finite set EE, the preorder polytope associated to τ\tau is the polytope 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} in ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E} defined by the linear inequalities xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0 for e∈Ee\in E and

(2) ∑e∈ℐxe≤|ℐ|\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{I}}}x_{e}\leq|{\mathcal{I}}|

for all order ideals ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau. This definition recovers and extends the definition of arbor polytopes. Indeed, every arbor σ\sigma can be considered as a preorder τ\tau having the root of σ\sigma as the maximum vertex. Then, for every vertex vv of σ\sigma the set 𝒟⁡(v)\mathscr{D}(v) is a principal order ideal of τ\tau and inequalities of the form (2) associated to nonprincipal order ideals of τ\tau are consequences (namely sums) of inequalities associated to principal order ideals.

It is not obvious that preorder polytopes are lattice polytopes and no longer true that they are always simple. Our first main result shows that preorder polytopes are indeed lattice polytopes which form a subclass of the class of generalized permutohedra [Pos09].

Theorem 1.4.

Let τ\tau be a preorder on an nn-element set. Then, 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is an nn-dimensional lattice polytope which is unimodularly equivalent to a generalized permutohedron.

An advantage of considering preorder polytopes, compared to the more restrictive class of arbor polytopes, is that there is a natural notion of duality for preorders. This notion allows for a generalization of Theorem 1.3 which we call Ehrhart-Zeta duality. Another obvious advantage is that the new setting allows for more interesting examples. We denote by τ∗\tau^{\ast} the dual of the preorder τ\tau and define the poset PτP_{\tau} of lattice points of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} as we did for arbors. The following statement is the second main result of this paper.

Theorem 1.5.

Let τ\tau be a preorder on an nn-element set EE.

  • (a)

    The Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is given by the formula

    Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,t)=∑(ae)∈Pτ∗∏e∈E(t+ae−1ae),{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=\sum_{(a_{e})\in P_{\tau^{\ast}}}\prod_{e\in E}\binom{t+a_{e}-1}{a_{e}},

    where the sum ranges over all lattice points (ae)(a_{e}) of 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}. In particular, the number of lattice points of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is equal to that of 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}.

    The normalized volume of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is equal to the number of words w∈Enw\in E^{n} such that for every order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau, the elements of ℐ{\mathcal{I}} appear a total of at least |ℐ||{\mathcal{I}}| times in ww.

  • (b)

    The Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} and the zeta polynomial of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} are related by the identity

    Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,t)=𝒵⁡(Pτ∗,t+1).{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)={\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau^{\ast}},t+1).

The proofs of both results rely on the theory of generalized permutohedra [Pos09]. An interesting feature of our study of preorder polytopes is the variety of conjectures on their lattice point enumeration that can be stated, some of which extend Conjecture 1.1 and (partly) Conjecture 1.2 on arbor polytopes.

The content and structure of this paper can be summarized as follows. Section 2 discusses notation and reviews basic definitions and background on poset and preposet combinatorics, Ehrhart theory of lattice polytopes, generalized permutohedra and related topics. Section 3 establishes basic properties of preorder polytopes and their posets of lattice points. Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 are proven in Sections 3 and 4, respectively, by applying results from the theory of generalized permutohedra [Pos09]. Section 4 also conjectures a stronger form of Ehrhart-Zeta duality, as well as a combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of any preorder polytope which refines that of the normalized volume given by Theorem 1.5 (see Conjectures 4.2 and 4.4) and provides partial results and a formula for the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial. Ehrhart polynomials of preorder polytopes may have nonreal complex roots. However, a weaker property (called magic positivity) which implies the real-rootedness of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial is conjectured in Section 4 (see Conjecture 4.8).

Section 5 discusses the natural extension of Conjecture 1.1 for preorder polytopes and conjectures the γ\gamma-positivity and real-rootedness of hh-polynomials of preorders, as well as their invariance under duality. Section 6 studies reflexive polytopes which can be obtained as Minkowski sums of preorder polytopes and standard simplices. Section 7 provides a formula for the double Ehrhart polynomial of a preorder polytope and the standard simplex and conjectures an identity (see Conjecture 7.2) which is stronger than Conjecture 4.4. Section 8 briefly discusses an important enumerative invariant of the poset of lattice points of a preorder polytope, namely the MM-triangle. Section 9 discusses some interesting examples and confirms some of the conjectures of this paper for them.

2. Preliminaries

This section establishes notation to be followed throughout the paper and reviews definitions and background on the combinatorics of partial orders and preorders, lattice polytopes and generalized permutohedra. More information about these topics can be found in [Hi92, Sta96, Sta11, Pos09].

2.1. Notation

Let EE be a nonempty finite set. We will denote by (𝐞e)e∈E{({\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e})}_{e\in E} the standard basis of the space ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}. We will use boldface letters to denote vectors 𝐱=(xe)e∈E\mathbf{x}=(x_{e})_{e\in E} of ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}, or collections of real numbers. We will denote by |𝐱||\mathbf{x}| the sum of the coordinates of a point 𝐱∈ℝE\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{E} and by |S||S| or #​S\#S the cardinality of a finite set SS.

2.2. Preorders

Let EE be a nonempty finite set. A preorder on EE is defined as a reflexive and transitive relation ≤\leq on EE. Declaring two elements a,b∈Ea,b\in E to be equivalent if a≤ba\leq b and b≤ab\leq a, one gets an equivalence relation on EE. The induced order on the set of equivalence classes, which we call vertices, is a partial order denoted by ⪯\preceq. Thus, a preorder ≤\leq on the ground set EE can also be defined as a partial order ⪯\preceq on the set of blocks of a partition of EE. We will depict ≤\leq by the Hasse diagram [Sta11, Section 3.1] of the associated partial order ⪯\preceq (where, as usual, the order increases from bottom to top). In the language of species [BLL98], we are working with the composition of the species of partial orders with that of nonempty finite sets. Preorders on a finite set EE are in one-to-one correspondence with topologies on EE [Sta11, Exercise 3.3]. We will usually denote preordered finite sets by small greek letters. We will refer to the cardinality of the ground set EE as the size of a preorder on EE and to the cardinality of a vertex as the size of this vertex. Figure 1 shows the Hasse diagram of a preorder of size 5; there is one vertex of size two and three single element vertices.

Basic constructions for posets [Sta11, Sections 3.1-3.2], such as disjoint unions, ordinal sums, duality, order ideals and filters and principal order ideals and filters, extend naturally to preorders. For example, an order ideal of a preorder on the ground set EE is defined as any subset ℐ⊆E{\mathcal{I}}\subseteq E such that for every b∈ℐb\in{\mathcal{I}} we have a∈ℐa\in{\mathcal{I}} for every a∈Ea\in E with a≤ba\leq b. Thus, order ideals are unions of vertices which are ideals of the associated partial order ⪯\preceq. Similarly, an order filter (or dual order ideal) is defined as any subset 𝒥⊆E{\mathcal{J}}\subseteq E such that for every a∈𝒥a\in{\mathcal{J}} we have b∈𝒥b\in{\mathcal{J}} for every b∈Eb\in E with a≤ba\leq b. We will denote by 𝒟⁡(e)\mathscr{D}(e) (respectively, 𝒰⁡(e)\mathscr{U}(e)) the principal order ideal (respectively, principal order filter) generated by e∈Ee\in E. We will sometimes abuse notation and write 𝒟⁡(v)\mathscr{D}(v) and 𝒰⁡(v)\mathscr{U}(v) for a vertex vv.

A preorder ≤\leq on EE is called a chain if a≤ba\leq b or b≤ab\leq a for all a,b∈Ea,b\in E (equivalently, the induced partial order ⪯\preceq is a total order). Chains are preorders associated to linear arbors [Cha25b, Section 4]; the corresponding arbor polytopes were studied in [Ath25] and called composition polytopes.

2.3. Poset combinatorics

Let (P,⪯)(P,\preceq) be a finite poset and let dd be the length (one less than the cardinality) of the longest chain in PP. The zeta polynomial [Sta11, Section 3.12] of PP is the unique polynomial 𝒵⁡(P,t){\mathcal{Z}}(P,t) with the property that 𝒵⁡(P,m+1){\mathcal{Z}}(P,m+1) is equal to the number of mm-element multichains in PP, meaning sequences (p1,p2,…,pm)(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{m}) of elements of PP such that p1⪯p2⪯⋯⪯pmp_{1}\preceq p_{2}\preceq\cdots\preceq p_{m}, for every m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}. The degree of 𝒵⁡(P,t){\mathcal{Z}}(P,t) is equal to dd and the leading coefficient is equal to the number of (necessarily maximal) chains of PP of length dd, divided by d!d!. We say that PP is graded if all maximal chains in PP have length dd.

2.4. Ehrhart theory

Let 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} be a dd-dimensional lattice polytope in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (thus, every vertex of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} belongs to ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}). The Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} is the unique polynomial Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) with the property that Ehr⁡(𝒬,m)=#⁡(m​𝒬∩ℕn){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},m)=\#(m{\mathcal{Q}}\cap\mathbb{N}^{n}) for every m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}. The Ehrhart polynomial Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) has degree dd and thus

(3) ∑m≥0Ehr⁡(𝒬,m)​tm=h∗​(𝒬,t)(1−t)d+1\sum_{m\geq 0}{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},m)t^{m}=\frac{h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t)}{(1-t)^{d+1}}

for some polynomial h∗​(𝒬,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t) of degree at most dd, called the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial. The coefficients of h∗​(𝒬,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t) are in fact nonnegative integers [Hi92, Theorem 33.9] [Sta96, Section I.5]. The sequence h∗​(𝒬)=(h0∗​(𝒬),h1∗​(𝒬),…,hd∗​(𝒬))h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}})=(h^{\ast}_{0}({\mathcal{Q}}),h^{\ast}_{1}({\mathcal{Q}}),\dots,h^{\ast}_{d}({\mathcal{Q}})) of coefficients of h∗​(𝒬,t)=∑i=0dhi∗​(𝒬)​tih^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}h^{\ast}_{i}({\mathcal{Q}})t^{i} is the h∗h^{\ast}-vector of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}}. The leading coefficient of Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) is equal to the dd-dimensional volume of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}}. Multiplied by d!d!, this number is a positive integer called the normalized volume; it is equal to the sum of the entries of the h∗h^{\ast}-vector. Thus, the normalized volume is refined by the h∗h^{\ast}-vector.

The polytope 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} is said to be Ehrhart positive if all coefficients of Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) are nonnegative. Finding classes of Ehrhart positive lattice polytopes is a very interesting problem [FH24, Liu19]. Following [FH24], we say that Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) is magic positive if

Ehr⁡(𝒬,t)=∑i=0dci​ti​(1+t)d−i{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}c_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{d-i}

for some nonnegative real numbers c0,c1,…,cdc_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{d}. By a theorem of Brändén [Bra06, Theorem 4.2], this property (which is stronger than Ehrhart positivity) implies that h∗​(𝒬,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t) has only real roots.

2.5. Generalized permutohedra

We briefly recall, with slightly adapted notation, the definitions and some basic results from Postnikov’s theory of generalized permutohedra, as introduced in [Pos09]. This involves two distinct notions, namely generalized permutohedra and the subclass of YY-type generalized permutohedra.

Let EE be a nonempty finite set. For a nonempty subset II of EE, the standard simplex ΔI\Delta_{I} is the convex hull of the set of standard basis vectors {𝐞e:e∈I}\{{\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e}:e\in I\}. YY-type generalized permutohedra are defined as Minkowski sums of scaled standard simplices. More precisely, given a collection 𝐲={yI}I\mathbf{y}={\{y_{I}\}}_{I} of nonnegative real numbers indexed by nonempty subsets of EE,

(4) 𝒫y​(𝐲)=∑∅≠I⊆EyI​ΔI{\mathcal{P}}^{y}(\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\varnothing\not=I\subseteq E}y_{I}\Delta_{I}

is the YY-type generalized permutohedron associated to 𝐲\mathbf{y}.

On the other hand, generalized permutohedra are defined by linear equations and inequalities as follows. Given a collection 𝐳={zI}I\mathbf{z}={\{z_{I}\}}_{I} of nonnegative real numbers indexed by nonempty subsets of EE,

(5) 𝒫z(𝐳)={(xe)∈ℝE|∑e∈Exe=zE,∑i∈Ixi≥zI∀I≠∅}{\mathcal{P}}^{z}(\mathbf{z})=\bigg\{(x_{e})\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\biggm|\sum_{e\in E}x_{e}=z_{E},\quad\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}\geq z_{I}\quad\forall I\not=\varnothing\bigg\}

is the generalized permutohedron associated to 𝐳\mathbf{z}. By [Pos09, Proposition 6.3], every YY-type generalized permutohedron is a generalized permutohedron. More precisely, defining the collection 𝐳\mathbf{z} from the collection 𝐲\mathbf{y} by setting

(6) zJ=∑∅≠I⊆JyIz_{J}=\sum_{\varnothing\not=I\subseteq J}y_{I}

for nonempty J⊆EJ\subseteq E, there is an equality of polytopes: 𝒫y​(𝐲)=𝒫z​(𝐳){\mathcal{P}}^{y}(\mathbf{y})={\mathcal{P}}^{z}(\mathbf{z}).

We now present a basic formula from [Pos09] for the Ehrhart polynomial of an integral YY-type generalized permutohedron. Let us consider nonempty subsets I0,I1,…,ImI_{0},I_{1},\dots,I_{m} of EE and numbers y0,y1,…,ym∈ℕy_{0},y_{1},\dots,y_{m}\in\mathbb{N}. It is convenient to consider the bipartite graph GG with m+1m+1 vertices ℓ0,ℓ1,…,ℓm\ell_{0},\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m} on the left side and vertices rer_{e} for e∈Ee\in E on the right side for which ℓj\ell_{j} is adjacent to rer_{e} if and only if e∈Ije\in I_{j}. A sequence (a0,a1,…,am)∈ℕm+1(a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{m})\in\mathbb{N}^{m+1} is called GG-draconian [Pos09, Definition 9.2] if a0+a1+⋯+am=|E|−1a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{m}=|E|-1 and

(7) 1+∑α∈𝒜aα≤#​⋃α∈𝒜Iα1+\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal{A}}}a_{\alpha}\leq\#\bigcup_{\alpha\in{\mathcal{A}}}I_{\alpha}

for every nonempty 𝒜⊆{0,1,…,m}{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,m\}. The following statement is a consequence of [Pos09, Theorem 11.3].

Theorem 2.1 ([Pos09]).

Assume that the bipartite graph GG just described has no isolated vertices and that I0=EI_{0}=E. Then, for all nonnegative integers yjy_{j}, the Ehrhart polynomial of the YY-type generalized permutohedron

𝒬=∑j=0myj​ΔIj{\mathcal{Q}}=\sum_{j=0}^{m}y_{j}\Delta_{I_{j}}

in ℝ≥0E\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{E} is given, by the formula

Ehr⁡(𝒬,t)=∑(a0,a1,…,am)∈𝒢G(y0​t+a0a0)​∏i=1m(yi​t+ai−1ai),{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t)=\sum_{(a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{m})\in{\mathcal{G}}_{G}}\binom{y_{0}t+a_{0}}{a_{0}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\binom{y_{i}t+a_{i}-1}{a_{i}},

where 𝒢G{\mathcal{G}}_{G} stands for the set of GG-draconian sequences. In particular, 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} is Ehrhart positive.

3. Basic properties

This section establishes basic properties of preorder polytopes and their posets of lattice points and proves Theorem 1.4. Throughout this and the following sections (unless stated otherwise), τ\tau will be a preorder of size nn on the ground set EE; we assume that EE does not contain 0.

3.1. Elementary properties

We recall that 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is defined by xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0 for every e∈Ee\in E and the linear inequalities (2) for all order ideals ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau, where (xe)(x_{e}) are the standard coordinates of ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}. For our running example from Figure 1, these inequalities are

xa+xc\displaystyle x_{a}+x_{c} ≤2\displaystyle\leq 2
xb\displaystyle x_{b} ≤1\displaystyle\leq 1
xa+xb+xc+xe\displaystyle x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}+x_{e} ≤4\displaystyle\leq 4
xb+xd\displaystyle x_{b}+x_{d} ≤2\displaystyle\leq 2
xa+xb+xc+xd+xe\displaystyle x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}+x_{d}+x_{e} ≤5.\displaystyle\leq 5.

Since EE is an order ideal of τ\tau, one of the linear inequalities defining 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is

∑e∈Exe≤n\sum_{e\in E}x_{e}\leq n

and hence 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is indeed a bounded polyhedron in ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}. Clearly, one may disregard the inequalities (2) associated to order ideals which are disconnected as subgraphs of the Hasse diagram of τ\tau, since these are implied by the ones associated to connected order ideals.

Remark 3.1.

(a) Contrary to the situation with arbor polytopes [Cha25b], preorder polytopes are not necessarily simple. This property fails already for the three-element poset {a,b,c}\{a,b,c\} with relations a≺ba\prec b and a≺ca\prec c. The preorder polytope for Figure 1 is not simple either; its ff-vector is (1,27,69,72,38,10,1)(1,27,69,72,38,10,1).

(b) The polytope QτQ_{\tau} is an anti-blocking polytope, in the sense of [Fu71]; see also [Sch86, Section 9.3]. This means that Qτ⊂ℝ≥0EQ_{\tau}\subset\mathbb{R}^{E}_{\geq 0} and 𝐲∈𝒬τ⇒𝐱∈𝒬τ\mathbf{y}\in{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}\Rightarrow\mathbf{x}\in{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} whenever 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝ≥0E\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{E}_{\geq 0} with 𝐱≤𝐲\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{y} coordinatewise. ∎

3.2. Preorder polytopes as generalized permutohedra

This section shows that every preorder polytope is unimodularly equivalent to a generalized permutohedron and deduces Theorem 1.4. This construction, which is explicit, will be essential for other results of this paper as well. We will work with a larger family of polytopes than that of preorder polytopes, since this will be convenient in Sections 6 and 7.

For I⊆EI\subseteq E, let us denote by 𝚫I\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{I} the lattice simplex in ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E} with vertices the basis vectors 𝐞e{\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e} for e∈Ie\in I and the zero vector of ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}. For a vertex vv of τ\tau, let us denote by 𝓤v\boldsymbol{{\mathcal{U}}}_{v} the |v||v|th Minkowski power of the simplex 𝚫𝒰⁡(v)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\mathscr{U}(v)}, where 𝒰⁡(v)\mathscr{U}(v) is the principal order filter of τ\tau generated by vv (thus, 𝒰⁡(v)\mathscr{U}(v) is a union of vertices). Given r,s∈ℕr,s\in\mathbb{N}, we consider the Minkowski sum

(8) 𝒬τ​(r,s)=r​∑v𝓤v+s​𝚫E{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s)=r\sum_{v}\boldsymbol{{\mathcal{U}}}_{v}+s\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{E}

in ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}, where the sum ranges over all vertices vv of τ\tau.

Proposition 3.2.

The polytope 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) is unimodularly equivalent to the YY-type generalized permutohedron

r​∑v𝒰v+s​ΔE⊔{0}r\sum_{v}{\mathcal{U}}_{v}+s\Delta_{E\sqcup\{0\}}

in ℝE⊔{0}\mathbb{R}^{E\sqcup\{0\}}, where the sum ranges over all vertices vv of τ\tau and 𝒰v{\mathcal{U}}_{v} is the |v||v|th Minkowski power of the simplex Δ𝒰⁡(v)⊔{0}\Delta_{\mathscr{U}(v)\sqcup\{0\}} in ℝE⊔{0}\mathbb{R}^{E\sqcup\{0\}}.

Proof.

The projection ρ:ℝE⊔{0}→ℝE\rho:\mathbb{R}^{E\sqcup\{0\}}\to\mathbb{R}^{E} which forgets the zeroth coordinate induces a bijection from the hyperplane consisting of all points in ℝE⊔{0}\mathbb{R}^{E\sqcup\{0\}} with sum of coordinates equal to 1 onto ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E} and a unimodular equivalence between the lattice simplices ΔI⊔{0}⊂ℝE⊔{0}\Delta_{I\sqcup\{0\}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{E\sqcup\{0\}} and 𝚫I⊂ℝE\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{I}\subset\mathbb{R}^{E} for every I⊆EI\subseteq E. Thus, ρ\rho induces the claimed unimodular equivalence as well. ∎

Let us define a collection 𝐲=𝐲⁡(r,s)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{y}(r,s) of nonnegative integers, indexed by nonempty subsets of E⊔{0}E\sqcup\{0\}, by yI=0y_{I}=0 for every nonempty I⊆EI\subseteq E and

(9) yI⊔{0}={r​|v|+s​δI,E,if​I=𝒰⁡(v)​for some vertex​v​of​τ,s​δI,E,otherwisey_{I\sqcup\{0\}}=\begin{cases}r|v|+s\delta_{I,E},\text{if}\ I=\mathscr{U}(v)\ \text{for some vertex}\ v\ \text{of}\ \tau,\\ s\delta_{I,E},\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

for every I⊆EI\subseteq E, where

δI,E={1,if​I=E,0, otherwise.\delta_{I,E}=\begin{cases}1,\text{if}\ I=E,\\ 0,\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

We have just shown that 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) can be identified with the YY-type generalized permutohedron 𝒫y​(𝐲){\mathcal{P}}^{y}(\mathbf{y}). The following statement describes explicitly 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) in terms of linear inequalities.

Proposition 3.3.

The polytope 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) is defined by the inequalities xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0 for every e∈Ee\in E and

(10) ∑e∈ℐxe≤r​|ℐ|+s\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{I}}}x_{e}\leq r|{\mathcal{I}}|+s

for every order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau. In particular, 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) coincides with the preorder polytope 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} for r=1r=1 and s=0s=0.

Proof.

Let 𝐳=𝐳⁡(r,s)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}(r,s) be the collection of nonnegative integers, indexed by nonempty subsets of E⊔{0}E\sqcup\{0\}, defined by (6). Then, zI=0z_{I}=0 for every nonempty I⊆EI\subseteq E and

zI⊔{0}=r(∑v:𝒰⁡(v)⊆I|v|)+sδI,Ez_{I\sqcup\{0\}}=r\left(\,\sum_{v\,:\,\mathscr{U}(v)\subseteq I}|v|\right)+s\delta_{I,E}

for every I⊆EI\subseteq E. In particular,

(11) zE⊔{0}=r⁡(∑v|v|)+s=r​n+s,z_{E\sqcup\{0\}}=r\left(\,\sum_{v}|v|\right)+s=rn+s,

where the sum ranges over all vertices vv of τ\tau. By (5), the unique linear equation defining the generalized permutohedron 𝒫y​(𝐲){\mathcal{P}}^{y}(\mathbf{y}) becomes

(12) x0+∑e∈Exe=r​n+s,x_{0}+\sum_{e\in E}x_{e}=rn+s,

which we will use to eliminate x0x_{0} in the linear inequalities associated with nonempty subsets of E⊔{0}E\sqcup\{0\}. Clearly, the linear inequalities of (5) for nonempty I⊆EI\subseteq E amount to xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0 for every e∈Ee\in E, since zI=0z_{I}=0 for all such II.

We now consider a subset J⊔{0}J\sqcup\{0\}, where J⊆EJ\subseteq E; the associated inequality is

(13) x0+∑e∈Jxe≥zJ⊔{0}.x_{0}+\sum_{e\in J}x_{e}\geq z_{J\sqcup\{0\}}.

Let 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} be the maximal order filter of τ\tau contained in JJ; in other words, 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} is the union of all vertices vv of τ\tau such that 𝒰⁡(v)⊆J\mathscr{U}(v)\subseteq J. Then,

zJ⊔{0}=r(∑v:𝒰⁡(v)⊆J|v|)+sδJ,E=r|𝒥|+sδJ,Ez_{J\sqcup\{0\}}=r\left(\,\sum_{v\,:\,\mathscr{U}(v)\subseteq J}|v|\right)+s\delta_{J,E}=r|{\mathcal{J}}|+s\delta_{J,E}

and hence, in view of Equation (12), the inequality (13) is equivalent to

where II and ℐ{\mathcal{I}} are the complements of JJ and 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} in EE, respectively. The special case when J=EJ=E gives a trivial inequality and can be ignored. Otherwise, this inequality yields (10) when J=𝒥J={\mathcal{J}} is an order filter of τ\tau itself, so that I=ℐI={\mathcal{I}} is an order ideal. It is also implied by (10) since I⊆ℐI\subseteq{\mathcal{I}} and hence

∑e∈Ixe≤∑e∈ℐxe.\sum_{e\in I}x_{e}\leq\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{I}}}x_{e}.

Since complementation induces a one-to-one correspendence between order ideals and order filters of τ\tau, the proof follows from our considerations and Proposition 3.2. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Combining Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 shows that 𝒬τ=𝒬τ​(1,0){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}={\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(1,0) is a lattice polytope which is unimodularly equivalent to a YY-type generalized permutohedron. The dimension of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is equal to nn since it contains the nn-dimensional cube [0,1]E[0,1]^{E}. ∎

3.3. Lattice points

As mentioned in the introduction, we denote by PτP_{\tau} the set of lattice points of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} and consider it a subposet of the product poset ℕE\mathbb{N}^{E}. Thus, for elements 𝐚=(ae)\mathbf{a}=(a_{e}) and 𝐛=(be)\mathbf{b}=(b_{e}) of PτP_{\tau} we have 𝐚⪯𝐛\mathbf{a}\preceq\mathbf{b} if and only if ae≤bea_{e}\leq b_{e} for every e∈Ee\in E. In our running example from Figure 1, PτP_{\tau} has cardinality 92.

The poset PτP_{\tau} is an order ideal of ℕE\mathbb{N}^{E}. In particular, the zero vector 𝟎\mathbf{0} is its minimum element and every interval [𝟎,x][\mathbf{0},x] is a product of chains. Moreover, PτP_{\tau} is graded with rank function given by the sum of coordinates. The following multiplicative property is a direct consequence of the relevant definitions.

Proposition 3.4.

Let τ\tau be the disjoint union of two preorders τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2}. Then:

  • (a)

    𝒬τ=𝒬τ1×𝒬τ2{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}={\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau_{1}}\times{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau_{2}}.

  • (b)

    Pτ=Pτ1×Pτ2P_{\tau}=P_{\tau_{1}}\times P_{\tau_{2}}.

The polytope 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} has no interior lattice points, but it does have some once scaled by 2, such as the point (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1). Let us call upper boundary of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} the set of its points which satisfy at least one of the defining inequalities (2) as an equality and denote this set by ∂^​(𝒬τ)\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}).

Proposition 3.5.

The number of interior lattice points of 2​𝒬τ2{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is equal to the number of lattice points of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} not in ∂^​(𝒬τ)\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}).

Proof.

There is a bijection between the two sets of lattice points, given by translation by the vector (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1). ∎

4. Ehrhart theory

This section studies the Ehrhart polynomial of the preorder polytope 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} and proves Theorem 1.5. An explicit combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is conjectured, partial results are given in this direction and a conjectural generalization of part (b) of Theorem 1.5 (Ehrhart-Zeta duality) is included.

4.1. Ehrhart-Zeta duality

Let us define a bipartite graph GτG_{\tau} with n+1n+1 left and n+1n+1 right vertices as follows. There are vertices ℓe\ell_{e} on the left side and rer_{e} on the right side, for e∈E⊔{0}e\in E\sqcup\{0\}. Vertex ℓ0\ell_{0} is connected by an edge to all vertices on the right and r0r_{0} is connected by an edge to all vertices on the left. For every e∈Ee\in E, there are edges from ℓe\ell_{e} to all vertices rfr_{f} such that ff belongs to the principal order filter 𝒰⁡(e)\mathscr{U}(e) of τ\tau. The graph GτG_{\tau} has no isolated vertex; it is shown in Figure 2 in the case of our running example from Figure 1. We set

Ie={f∈E⊔{0}∣{ℓe,rf}​is an edge of​Gτ}I_{e}=\{f\in E\sqcup\{0\}\mid\{\ell_{e},r_{f}\}\ \text{is an edge of}\ G_{\tau}\}

for e∈E⊔{0}e\in E\sqcup\{0\}. Equivalently, Ie=𝒰⁡(e)⊔{0}I_{e}=\mathscr{U}(e)\sqcup\{0\} for every e∈Ee\in E and I0=E⊔{0}I_{0}=E\sqcup\{0\}. According to Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, the preorder polytope 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is unimodularly equivalent to the YY-type generalized permutohedron

∑e∈E⊔{0}ye​ΔIe\sum_{e\in E\sqcup\{0\}}y_{e}\Delta_{I_{e}}

in ℝ≥0E⊔{0}\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{E\sqcup\{0\}} with parameters y0=0y_{0}=0 and ye=1y_{e}=1 for every e∈Ee\in E. To apply Theorem 2.1, we need to understand the GτG_{\tau}-draconian sequences.

Lemma 4.1.

A sequence (ae)e∈E⊔{0}∈ℕE⊔{0}(a_{e})_{e\in E\sqcup\{0\}}\in\mathbb{N}^{E\sqcup\{0\}} is GτG_{\tau}-draconian if and only if

(14) a0+∑e∈Eae=na_{0}+\sum_{e\in E}a_{e}=n

and (ae)e∈E(a_{e})_{e\in E} is a lattice point of 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}.

Proof.

According to the definition (see Section 2.5), (ae)e∈E⊔{0}∈ℕE⊔{0}(a_{e})_{e\in E\sqcup\{0\}}\in\mathbb{N}^{E\sqcup\{0\}} is GτG_{\tau}-draconian if and only if Equation (14) is valid and (7) holds for every nonempty 𝒜⊆E⊔{0}{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq E\sqcup\{0\}. Let us analyze these inequalities and show that some of them are superflous.

Since I0=E⊔{0}I_{0}=E\sqcup\{0\}, if 0∈𝒜0\in{\mathcal{A}} then (7) becomes ∑e∈𝒜ae≤n\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{A}}}a_{e}\leq n, which is a consequence of (14). Thus, we may assume that 𝒜⊆E{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq E. Then, we get

(15) ∑e∈𝒜ae≤|𝒰⁡(𝒜)|,\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{A}}}a_{e}\leq|\mathscr{U}({\mathcal{A}})|,

where 𝒰⁡(𝒜)\mathscr{U}({\mathcal{A}}) is the order filter of τ\tau generated by 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. In particular, if 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is an order filter 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} itself, so that 𝒰⁡(𝒜)=𝒥\mathscr{U}({\mathcal{A}})={\mathcal{J}}, we get

(16) ∑e∈𝒥ae≤|𝒥|.\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{J}}}a_{e}\leq|{\mathcal{J}}|.

In general, ∑e∈𝒜ae≤∑e∈𝒰⁡(𝒜)ae\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{A}}}a_{e}\leq\sum_{e\in\mathscr{U}({\mathcal{A}})}a_{e}, so (15) follows from (16) for 𝒥=𝒰⁡(𝒜){\mathcal{J}}=\mathscr{U}({\mathcal{A}}). As a conclusion, the GτG_{\tau}-draconian conditions are equivalent to Equation (14) and the validity of (16) for all order filters 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} of τ\tau. The latter means that (ae)e∈E(a_{e})_{e\in E} is a lattice point of 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}} and the proof follows. ∎

We are now in a position to prove Theorem 1.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

The formula of part (a) for the Ehrhart polynomial follows directly by combining Theorem 2.1, applied to the graph GτG_{\tau} for the parameters y0=0y_{0}=0 and ye=1y_{e}=1 for every e∈Ee\in E, with Lemma 4.1.

To deduce part (b), let us count the mm-multichains in the poset Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} for m≥1m\geq 1. One can can condition on the top element 𝐚=(ae)e∈E∈Pτ∗\mathbf{a}=(a_{e})_{e\in E}\in P_{\tau^{\ast}} of such a multichain. Since the interval [0,𝐚][0,\mathbf{a}] is isomorphic to a product of chains of lengths aea_{e}, the number of mm-multichains in Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} with top element 𝐚\mathbf{a} is equal to the product ∏e∈E(m+ae−1ae)\prod_{e\in E}\binom{m+a_{e}-1}{a_{e}}. As a result,

𝒵⁡(Pτ∗,m+1)=∑(ae)∈Pτ∗∏e∈E(m+ae−1ae){\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau^{\ast}},m+1)=\sum_{(a_{e})\in P_{\tau^{\ast}}}\prod_{e\in E}\binom{m+a_{e}-1}{a_{e}}

for every m≥1m\geq 1 and part (b) follows by comparison with the formula of part (a).

We may now deduce the last statement of part (a) as follows. By part (b), the normalized volume of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is equal to n!n! times the coefficient of tnt^{n} in 𝒵⁡(Pτ∗,t+1){\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau^{\ast}},t+1) and hence to the number of chains of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} of length nn (since Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} is graded of rank nn, these are exactly the maximal chains of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}}). To every such chain, one can associate the word of length nn in the alphabet EE which records at each step of the chain the unique coordinate which increases. The resulting map is one-to-one and, by definition of 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}, the words thus obtained are those words w∈Enw\in E^{n} such that the elements of any order ideal 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} of τ∗\tau^{\ast} appear at most |𝒥||{\mathcal{J}}| times in ww. Equivalently, the elements of any order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau should appear at least |ℐ||{\mathcal{I}}| times in ww. ∎

4.2. Matrix Ehrhart-Zeta duality

One can extend Ehrhart-Zeta duality in terms of infinite matrices as follows. For k,ℓ∈ℕk,\ell\in\mathbb{N} we denote by ∇τ(k,ℓ)\nabla_{\tau}(k,\ell) the number of kk-multichains in the poset of lattice points of ℓ​𝒬τ\ell{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} (where the order is induced from ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}, as usual). This function can be viewed as an infinite matrix with rows and columns indexed by nonnegative integers, every column of which is the sequence of values of a zeta polynomial. We have ∇τ(k,0)=∇τ(0,ℓ)=1\nabla_{\tau}(k,0)=\nabla_{\tau}(0,\ell)=1, ∇τ(k,1)=𝒵⁡(Pτ,k+1)\nabla_{\tau}(k,1)={\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},k+1) and ∇τ(1,ℓ)=Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,ℓ)\nabla_{\tau}(1,\ell)={\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},\ell) for all k,ℓ∈ℕk,\ell\in\mathbb{N}.

The following conjecture generalizes part (b) of Theorem 1.5; it has been verified by computer on certain finite pieces of ∇τ\nabla_{\tau} for preorders of size at most 5.

Conjecture 4.2.

The matrix ∇τ\nabla_{\tau} is the transpose of ∇τ∗\nabla_{\tau^{\ast}} for every preorder τ\tau.

A bijective proof of Ehrhart-Zeta duality was given for chain preorders in [Ath25]. This proof can be easily extended in the setting of the matrix Ehrhart-Zeta duality. We sketch the proof of the following proposition, which generalizes the first proof of Theorem 1.3 given in [Ath25, Section 4].

Proposition 4.3.

Conjecture 4.2 holds for all chain preorders.

Proof.

Let τ\tau be a chain v1≺v2≺⋯≺vpv_{1}\prec v_{2}\prec\cdots\prec v_{p} with vertices of sizes r1,r2,…,rpr_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{p}, respectively. We set si=r1+r2+⋯+ris_{i}=r_{1}+r_{2}+\cdots+r_{i} for 0≤i≤p0\leq i\leq p, so that where s0:=0s_{0}:=0 and sp=ns_{p}=n. We may assume that E={1,2,…,n}E=\{1,2,\dots,n\} with elements indexed so that 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is described by the inequalities xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and

x1+x2+⋯+xsi≤six_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}

for 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p. By [Ath25, Lemma 4.1], the kk-multichains in the poset of lattice points of ℓ​𝒬τ\ell{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} are in bijection with the points (a1,a2,…,an​k)∈ℕn​k(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{nk})\in\mathbb{N}^{nk} such that

(17) a1+a2+⋯+asi​k≤si​ℓa_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{s_{i}k}\leq s_{i}\ell

for 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p. Given such a point, for 0≤j≤n​ℓ0\leq j\leq n\ell we define bjb_{j} as the number of i∈{1,2,…,n​k}i\in\{1,2,\dots,nk\} such that a1+a2+⋯+ai=ja_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{i}=j. Then,

(18) b0+b1+⋯+bn​ℓ=n​kb_{0}+b_{1}+\cdots+b_{n\ell}=nk

and

(19) b0+b1+⋯+bsi​ℓ≥si​kb_{0}+b_{1}+\cdots+b_{s_{i}\ell}\geq s_{i}k

for 0≤i≤p0\leq i\leq p. Using Equation (18) to eliminate b0b_{0} we find that the solutions (a1,a2,…,an​k)∈ℕn​k(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{nk})\in\mathbb{N}^{nk} of the system of linear inequalities (17) are in bijection with the solutions (b1,b2,…,bn​ℓ)∈ℕn​ℓ(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n\ell})\in\mathbb{N}^{n\ell} of the system of linear inequalities

(20) bsi​ℓ+1+bsi​ℓ+2+⋯+bn​ℓ≤(n−si)​kb_{s_{i}\ell+1}+b_{s_{i}\ell+2}+\cdots+b_{n\ell}\leq(n-s_{i})k

for 0≤i≤p−10\leq i\leq p-1. By [Ath25, Lemma 4.1], and since 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}} is described by the inequalities xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and

xsi+1+xsi+2+⋯+xn≤n−six_{s_{i}+1}+x_{s_{i}+2}+\cdots+x_{n}\leq n-s_{i}

4.3. On the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial

We recall from Section 2.4 that the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) has nonnegative coefficients which sum to the normalized volume of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}. Thus, the following conjecture is a natural refinement of the second statement of Theorem 1.5 (a). We fix an arbitrary total order ≤\leq on the ground set EE and, given a word w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈Enw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in E^{n}, we denote by des⁡(w){\rm des}(w) the number of descents of ww, meaning indices i∈{1,2,…,n−1}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n-1\} such that wi>wi+1w_{i}>w_{i+1}. The following conjecture extends [AXY26, Conjecture 5.2] from arbor polytopes to all preorder polytopes.

Conjecture 4.4.

Let τ\tau be a preorder on a totally ordered nn-element set EE. Then

h∗​(𝒬τ,t)=∑w∈𝒲τtn−1−des⁡(w),h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau}}t^{n-1-{\rm des}(w)},

where 𝒲τ{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau} is the set of words w∈Enw\in E^{n} such that for every order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau, the elements of ℐ{\mathcal{I}} appear a total of at least |ℐ||{\mathcal{I}}| times in ww.

This conjecture has been verified by computer for all preorders of size at most 7. The motivation behind it comes from [AXY26, Theorem 1.5], which verifies it in the special case in which τ\tau is the preorder associated to an arbor which consists of a root of any size and several single element leaves.

A combinatorial interpretation of h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) which seems different from that of Conjecture 4.4 was given in [Ath25, Section 4] in the special case that the preorder τ\tau is a chain. The proof is based on the theory of pure shellability of posets and generalizes to all preorders with a minimum vertex. To state the result, it is convenient to assume that E={1,2,…,n}E=\{1,2,\dots,n\} is totally ordered as usual. Given a word w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈{1,2,…,n}nw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}^{n}, we denote by asc∗​(w){\rm asc}^{\ast}(w) the number of indices (called modified ascents) i∈{0,1,…,n−1}i\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} such that wi<wi+1w_{i}<w_{i+1}, where w0:=1w_{0}:=1. The following statement generalizes [Ath25, Proposition 4.2]. To avoid making too long of a digression we assume familiarity with the relevant parts of [Ath25, Section 4] and only sketch the proof, which directly extends that of [Ath25, Proposition 4.2].

Proposition 4.5.

Let τ\tau be a preorder of size nn on the ground set E={1,2,…,n}E=\{1,2,\dots,n\} which has a minimum vertex. Assuming that 1 belongs to this vertex we have

h∗​(𝒬τ,t)=∑w∈𝒲τtasc∗​(w),h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau}}t^{{\rm asc}^{\ast}(w)},

where 𝒲τ{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau} is as in Conjecture 4.4.

Proof.

As explained in the proof of [Ath25, Proposition 4.2] we have

h∗​(𝒬τ,t)=h⁡(Δ⁡(Pτ∗),t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=h(\Delta(P_{\tau^{\ast}}),t)

by Ehrhart-Zeta duality, where Δ⁡(Pτ∗)\Delta(P_{\tau^{\ast}}) stands for the order complex of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}}.

We consider the poset P^τ∗=Pτ∗∪{1^}\widehat{P}_{\tau^{\ast}}=P_{\tau^{\ast}}\cup\{\hat{1}\}, obtained from Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} by adding a maximum element 1^\hat{1}, and an integer valued edge labeling λ\lambda of this poset, defined as follows. For a cover relation (u,v)(u,v) of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} we set λ⁡(u,v)=i\lambda(u,v)=i, if uu and vv differ in the iith coordinate. We also set λ⁡(u,1^)=1\lambda(u,\hat{1})=1 for every maximal element u∈Pτu\in P_{\tau} and claim that λ\lambda is an EL-labeling. This means that, given any nonsingleton closed interval [u,v][u,v] of P^τ∗\widehat{P}_{\tau^{\ast}}, there is a unique rising (with respect to λ\lambda) maximal chain in [u,v][u,v] and that this chain is lexicographically least among all maximal chains of [u,v][u,v]. This is clear if v≠1^v\neq\hat{1}, since then the labels of the maximal chains of [u,v][u,v] are the permutations of a multiset. Suppose that v=1^v=\hat{1}. By assumption, τ∗\tau^{\ast} has a maximum vertex and this vertex contains 1. This implies that from the linear inequalities (2) which define 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}, only the one associated to the order ideal EE of τ∗\tau^{\ast} involves the variable x1x_{1}. As a result, there is a unique maximal chain in [u,1^][u,\hat{1}] with label (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1) and this chain is the only rising maximal chain of [u,1^][u,\hat{1}].

Since λ\lambda is EL, h⁡(Δ⁡(Pτ∗),t)h(\Delta(P_{\tau^{\ast}}),t) can be interpreted as the descent enumerator (with respect to λ\lambda) of the maximal chains of P^τ∗\widehat{P}_{\tau^{\ast}}. As already observed in the proof of Theorem 1.5, these chains are in bijection with the elements of 𝒲τ{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau} and the proof follows. ∎

The proof of Proposition 4.5 shows that the poset PτP_{\tau} is shellable, and hence Cohen-Macaulay (over ℤ\mathbb{Z} and any field), if τ\tau has a maximum vertex. This raises the following question.

Question 4.6.

Is the poset PτP_{\tau} shellable for every preorder τ\tau? Is it Cohen–Macaulay for every preorder τ\tau?

A formula for h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) may be derived from part (a) of Theorem 1.5 as follows.

Proposition 4.7.

Let τ\tau be a preorder of size nn on a totally ordered ground set EE. Then

h∗​(𝒬τ,t)=(1−t)n+∑w∈𝒲^τ∖{∅}(1−t)n−ℓ⁡(w)​tdes⁡(w),h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=(1-t)^{n}+\sum_{w\in\widehat{{\mathcal{W}}}_{\tau}\smallsetminus\{\varnothing\}}(1-t)^{n-\ell(w)}t^{{\rm des}(w)},

where 𝒲^τ\widehat{{\mathcal{W}}}_{\tau} is the set of words ww of length (number of letters) ℓ⁡(w)≤n\ell(w)\leq n with letters from EE such that for every order filter 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} of τ\tau, the elements of 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} appear a total of at most |𝒥||{\mathcal{J}}| times in ww.

Proof.

Given 𝐚=(ae)∈ℕE\mathbf{a}=(a_{e})\in\mathbb{N}^{E}, let us denote by 𝔖𝐚\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{a}} the set of permutations of the multiset which consists of aea_{e} copies of ee, for e∈Ee\in E. By part (a) of Theorem 1.5,

∑m≥0Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,m)​tm\displaystyle\sum_{m\geq 0}{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},m)t^{m} =1+∑m≥0Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,m+1)​tm+1\displaystyle=1+\sum_{m\geq 0}{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},m+1)t^{m+1}
=1+t​∑m≥0(∑(ae)∈Pτ∗∏e∈E(m+aeae))​tm\displaystyle=1+t\sum_{m\geq 0}\left(\,\sum_{(a_{e})\in P_{\tau^{\ast}}}\prod_{e\in E}\binom{m+a_{e}}{a_{e}}\right)t^{m}
=1+t​∑𝐚∈Pτ∗(∑w∈𝔖𝐚tdes⁡(w))/(1−t)1+|𝐚|,\displaystyle=1+t\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in P_{\tau^{\ast}}}\left(\,\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{a}}}t^{{\rm des}(w)}\right)/(1-t)^{1+|\mathbf{a}|},

where the third equality applies MacMahon’s formula [Mac04, p. 211]

∑m≥0(∏e∈E(m+aeae))​tm=∑w∈𝔖𝐚tdes⁡(w)(1−t)1+|𝐚|\sum_{m\geq 0}\left(\,\prod_{e\in E}\binom{m+a_{e}}{a_{e}}\right)t^{m}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{a}}}t^{{\rm des}(w)}}{(1-t)^{1+|\mathbf{a}|}}

for 𝐚=(ae)∈ℕE\mathbf{a}=(a_{e})\in\mathbb{N}^{E}. This computation shows that

h∗​(𝒬τ,t)=(1−t)n+1+t​∑𝐚∈Pτ∗(1−t)n−|𝐚|​∑w∈𝔖𝐚tdes⁡(w).h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=(1-t)^{n+1}+t\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in P_{\tau^{\ast}}}(1-t)^{n-|\mathbf{a}|}\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{a}}}t^{{\rm des}(w)}.

We now observe that the summand of the outer sum on the right-hand side for 𝐚=𝟎\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0} is equal to (1−t)n(1-t)^{n} and that 𝒲^τ\widehat{{\mathcal{W}}}_{\tau} is the disjoint union of the sets 𝔖𝐚\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{a}} for 𝐚∈Pτ∗\mathbf{a}\in P_{\tau^{\ast}} and the proof follows. ∎

As mentioned in the introduction, Ehrhart polynomials of preorder polytopes are not always real-rooted. For example, if τ\tau is a partial order consisting of a minimum element and two other elements incomparable to each other which cover it, then Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,t)=1+23​t/6+5​t2+13​t3/6{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=1+23t/6+5t^{2}+13t^{3}/6 has two nonreal complex roots. We conjecture that Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) has the weaker magic positivity property and hence that h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) is real-rooted.

Conjecture 4.8.

The Ehrhart polynomial Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) is magic positive for every preorder τ\tau. In particular, h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) is real-rooted.

This conjecture has been proven for the special class of the arbor polytopes studied in [AXY26] and also follows from [SP02, Theorem 13] when τ\tau is a chain with vertices of size one (in which case 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is the standard Pitman–Stanley polytope). The coefficients of the Ehrhart polynomial in the magic basis ti​(1+t)n−it^{i}(1+t)^{n-i}, multiplied by n!n!, have interesting combinatorial interpretations in both cases; see [AFM26, Section 1] [AXY26, Section 3] [GS06, Theorem 10.1]. Conjecture 4.8 has been verified by computer for all preorders of size at most 7.

4.4. On the zeta polynomial

Computational evidence suggests that (−1)n​𝒵​(Pτ,−1)(-1)^{n}{\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},-1) is equal to the number of maximal elements of PτP_{\tau}. A refined conjecture may be formulated using the notion of qq-zeta polynomial introduced in [Cha25a]. Given a finite graded poset PP with rank function ρ:P→ℕ\rho:P\to\mathbb{N}, it was shown in [Cha25a] that there exists a polynomial 𝒵q​(P,t)∈ℚ⁡(q)​[t]{\mathcal{Z}}_{q}(P,t)\in\mathbb{Q}(q)[t] such that

𝒵q​(P,[m]q)=∑p1⪯p2⪯⋯⪯pm−1qρ⁡(p1)+ρ⁡(p2)+⋯+ρ⁡(pm−1){\mathcal{Z}}_{q}(P,[m]_{q})=\sum_{p_{1}\preceq p_{2}\preceq\cdots\preceq p_{m-1}}q^{\rho(p_{1})+\rho(p_{2})+\cdots+\rho(p_{m-1})}

for every integer m≥2m\geq 2, where the sum ranges over all multichains p1⪯p2⪯⋯⪯pm−1p_{1}\preceq p_{2}\preceq\cdots\preceq p_{m-1} in PP and [m]q=(qm−1)/(q−1)[m]_{q}=(q^{m}-1)/(q-1) is the standard qq-analog of mm. Let us denote by Max⁡(P)\operatorname{Max}(P) the set of maximal elements of a finite poset PP.

Conjecture 4.9.

For every preorder τ\tau of size nn

(21) 𝒵q​(Pτ,[−1]q)=(−1)n​∑𝐚∈Max⁡(Pτ)q−cov⁡(𝐚),{\mathcal{Z}}_{q}(P_{\tau},[-1]_{q})=(-1)^{n}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\operatorname{Max}(P_{\tau})}q^{-\operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{a})},

where cov⁡(𝐚)\operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{a}) is the number of elements of PτP_{\tau} covered by 𝐚\mathbf{a} and [−1]q=−1/q[-1]_{q}=-1/q. In particular,

(22) 𝒵⁡(Pτ,−1)=(−1)n​#​Max⁡(Pτ){\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},-1)=(-1)^{n}\,\#\operatorname{Max}(P_{\tau})

for every preorder τ\tau of size nn.

This conjecture has been verified by computer for all preorders of size at most 6. For the example of Figure 1 we have 𝒵⁡(Pτ,−1)=−18{\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},-1)=-18 and

𝒵q(Pτ,[−1]q)=−(2q+1)(q2+4q+1)/q5{\mathcal{Z}}_{q}(P_{\tau},[-1]_{q})=-(2q+1)(q^{2}+4q+1)/q^{5}

and PτP_{\tau} has 18 maximal elements.

Remark 4.10.

(a) Equation (22) is a consequence of Conjecture 4.4. Indeed, we have 𝒵⁡(Pτ,−1)=Ehr⁡(𝒬τ∗,−2){\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},-1)={\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}},-2) by Ehrhart-Zeta duality and

Ehr⁡(𝒬τ∗,t)=∑i=0nhi∗​(𝒬τ∗)​(t+n−in){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}h^{\ast}_{i}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}})\binom{t+n-i}{n}

by Equation (3). Moreover, hn∗​(𝒬τ∗)=0h^{\ast}_{n}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}})=0 since 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}} has no interior lattice points and hence

Ehr⁡(𝒬τ∗,−2)=(−1)n​hn−1∗​(𝒬τ∗).{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}},-2)=(-1)^{n}\,h^{\ast}_{n-1}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}).

According to Conjecture 4.4, hn−1∗​(𝒬τ∗)h^{\ast}_{n-1}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}) is equal to the number of words w∈𝒲τ∗w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau^{\ast}} with no descent. These are the (weakly) increasing words w∈Enw\in E^{n} such that the elements of any order filter 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} of τ\tau appear a total of at least |𝒥||{\mathcal{J}}| times in ww. Equivalently, the elements of any order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of PτP_{\tau} should appear at most |ℐ||{\mathcal{I}}| times in ww. These words are obviously in bijection with the maximal elements of PτP_{\tau}.

(b) By Ehrhart reciprocity, (−1)n​Ehr​(𝒬τ∗,−2)(-1)^{n}\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}},-2) is equal to the number of lattice points in the interior of 2​𝒬τ∗2{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}. Thus, in view of Proposition 3.5, Equation (22) is equivalent to the statement that the number of maximal elements of PτP_{\tau} is equal to the number of lattice points of 𝒬τ∗{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}} not in the upper boundary ∂^​(𝒬τ∗)\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau^{\ast}}). ∎

Remark 4.11.

Equation (22) holds for every chain preorder τ\tau. To explain why, let us adopt the notation of the proof of Proposition 4.3. By part (b) of Remark 4.10, it suffices to show that the number of maximal elements of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} is equal to the number of lattice points of 𝒬τ∖∂^​(𝒬τ){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}\smallsetminus\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}). The maximal elements of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} are the tuples (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n} such that a1+a2+⋯+an=na_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=n and

asi+1+asi+2+⋯+an≤n−sia_{s_{i}+1}+a_{s_{i}+2}+\cdots+a_{n}\leq n-s_{i}

for 1≤i≤p−11\leq i\leq p-1 or, equivalently,

a1+a2+⋯+asi≥sia_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{s_{i}}\geq s_{i}

for 1≤i≤p−11\leq i\leq p-1. The lattice points of 𝒬τ∖∂^​(𝒬τ){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}\smallsetminus\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}) are the tuples (b1,b2,…,bn)∈ℕn(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n} such that

b1+b2+⋯+bsi<sib_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{s_{i}}<s_{i}

for 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p. Given a maximal element (a1,a2,…,an)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}}, for 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n we define bjb_{j} to be the number of indices i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n\} such that a1+a2+⋯+ai=j−1a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{i}=j-1. We leave it to the reader to verify that (b1,b2,…,bn)(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n}) is a lattice point of 𝒬τ∖∂^​(𝒬τ){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}\smallsetminus\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}) and that the resulting map is a bijection from the set of maximal elements of Pτ∗P_{\tau^{\ast}} to the set of lattice points of 𝒬τ∖∂^​(𝒬τ){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}\smallsetminus\hat{\partial}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}).

5. Lattice point enumeration

This section extends to preorder polytopes some conjectures of [Cha25b] on the lattice point enumeration of arbor polytopes. Throughout this and the following two sections, τ\tau continues to be a preorder of size nn on the ground set EE.

For 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n, we let hi​(τ)h_{i}(\tau) be the number of lattice points of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} which have exactly ii nonzero coordinates. The vector h⁡(τ)=(h0​(τ),h1​(τ),…,hn​(τ))h(\tau)=(h_{0}(\tau),h_{1}(\tau),\dots,h_{n}(\tau)) is called the hh-vector of τ\tau and the polynomial h⁡(τ,t)=∑i=0nhi​(τ)​tih(\tau,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}h_{i}(\tau)t^{i} is called the hh-polynomial. These concepts directly generalize the notion of hh-vector of an arbor, introduced in [Cha25b]. For the example of Figure 1 we have h⁡(τ)=(1,11,34,34,11,1)h(\tau)=(1,11,34,34,11,1). We note that h0​(τ)=h1​(τ)=1h_{0}(\tau)=h_{1}(\tau)=1. The following conjecture, the parts of which appear in the order of increasing strength, generalizes Conjecture 1.1 in [Cha25b]. For undefined terminology about simplicial polytopes, see [Sta96].

Conjecture 5.1.

For every preorder τ\tau of size nn:

  • (a)

    h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is palindromic, meaning that hi​(τ)=hn−i​(τ)h_{i}(\tau)=h_{n-i}(\tau) for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n.

  • (b)

    h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is palindromic and unimodal, meaning that hi​(τ)=hn−i​(τ)h_{i}(\tau)=h_{n-i}(\tau) for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n and h0​(τ)≤h1​(τ)≤⋯≤h⌊n/2⌋​(τ)h_{0}(\tau)\leq h_{1}(\tau)\leq\cdots\leq h_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(\tau).

  • (c)

    h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is equal to the hh-vector of an nn-dimensional simplicial polytope.

  • (d)

    h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is equal to the hh-vector of an nn-dimensional flag simplicial polytope.

For example, if τ\tau is the chain preorder of size nn having nn vertices of cardinality 1 or one vertex of cardinality nn, then the role of the flag simplicial polytope of part (d) can be played by the simplicial associahedron of of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n} and 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}, respectively; see Sections 7 and 8 of [Cha25b]. The following statement was implicitly conjectured for arbor polytopes in [Cha25b, Section 1.1].

Conjecture 5.2.

The polynomial h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t) is γ\gamma-positive, meaning that

h⁡(τ,t)=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋γi​(τ)​ti​(1+t)n−2​ih(\tau,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\gamma_{i}(\tau)t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}

for some nonnegative integers γ0​(τ),γ1​(τ),…,γ⌊n/2⌋​(τ)\gamma_{0}(\tau),\gamma_{1}(\tau),\dots,\gamma_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(\tau), for every preorder τ\tau of size nn. In particular, the vector h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is palindromic and unimodal.

A more optimistic conjecture is the following.

Conjecture 5.3.

The polynomial h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t) has only real roots for every preorder τ\tau.

The following statement substantially generalizes Conjecture 4.2 in [Cha25b].

Conjecture 5.4.

We have h⁡(τ)=h⁡(τ∗)h(\tau)=h(\tau^{\ast}) for every preorder τ\tau.

All previous conjectures, other than Conjecture 5.3, were proven for chain preorders in [Ath25]. They have been verified (together with Conjecture 5.3) in several other special cases in [AXY26] [Cha25b, Sections 7-10]; see also Section 9. The authors have verified by computer Conjecture 5.1 (c) for all preorders of size at most 7 and arbors of size at most 8, Conjectures 5.2 and 5.4 for all preorders of size at most 7 and Conjecture 5.3 for all preorders of size at most 7 and arbors of size at most 10.

Remark 5.5.

We do not know of a class of generalized permutohedra larger than that of preorder polytopes for which the hh-vector may be palindromic. For example, 𝒬=𝚫{1,2}+𝚫{2,3}+𝚫{3}{\mathcal{Q}}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\{1,2\}}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\{2,3\}}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\{3\}} is a YY-type generalized permutohedron in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} described by the inequalities x1,x2,x3≥0x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\geq 0 and

x1\displaystyle x_{1} ≤1\displaystyle\leq 1
x1+x2\displaystyle x_{1}+x_{2} ≤2\displaystyle\leq 2
x3\displaystyle x_{3} ≤2\displaystyle\leq 2
x1+x2+x3\displaystyle x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3} ≤3.\displaystyle\leq 3.

Counting its lattice points by the number of nonzero coordinates gives the vector (1,5,6,1)(1,5,6,1), which is not palindromic.

Remark 5.6.

One may naturally consider the formal power series

F⁡(τ,t)=h⁡(τ,t)(1−t)n+1.F(\tau,t)=\frac{h(\tau,t)}{{(1-t)}^{n+1}}.

The coefficients of F⁡(τ,t)F(\tau,t) are the values of a polynomial at nonnegative integers. Curiously, this polynomial has all its complex roots on the line Re(z)=−1/2\operatorname{Re}(z)=-1/2 for all preorders of size at most 7 and all arbors of size at most 8. The arbor

is the unique arbor of size 9 for which this property fails.

6. Preorder polytopes and reflexive polytopes

This section shows that, after suitable translation, the lattice polytope

𝒬τ​(1,1)=𝒬τ+𝚫E{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(1,1)={\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{E}

(see Section 3.2) is reflexive and investigates its properties. We recall that an nn-dimensional lattice polytope 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} having 𝟎\mathbf{0} in its interior is said to be reflexive if the polar dual of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} is also a lattice polytope. An equivalent condition [Hi92, Theorem 35.8] is that the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} is palindromic (of degree nn).

Let ℛτ{\mathcal{R}}_{\tau} denote the translation of 𝒬τ​(1,1){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(1,1) by the negative of the vector 𝟏=∑e∈E𝐞e∈ℝE\mathbf{1}=\sum_{e\in E}{\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{E}. By Proposition 3.3, 𝒬τ​(1,1){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(1,1) is defined by the inequalities xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0 for every e∈Ee\in E and

∑e∈ℐxe≤|ℐ|+1\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{I}}}x_{e}\leq|{\mathcal{I}}|+1

for every order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau. As a result, ℛτ{\mathcal{R}}_{\tau} is defined by the inequalities

(23) xe≥−1x_{e}\geq-1

for every e∈Ee\in E and

(24) ∑e∈ℐxe≤1\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{I}}}x_{e}\leq 1

for every order ideal ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau.

Proposition 6.1.

The lattice polytope ℛτ{\mathcal{R}}_{\tau} is reflexive for every preorder τ\tau.

Proof.

The inequalities (23) and (24) show that 𝟎\mathbf{0} is the unique interior lattice point of ℛτ{\mathcal{R}}_{\tau} and that its polar dual has vertices with integer coordinates. ∎

Let ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} be the reflexive polytope which is polar dual to ℛτ{\mathcal{R}}_{\tau}. By definition, ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} is the convex hull of the vectors −𝐞e-{\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e} for all e∈Ee\in E and ∑e∈ℐ𝐞e\sum_{e\in{\mathcal{I}}}{\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e} for all nonempty order ideals ℐ{\mathcal{I}} of τ\tau. Let us denote this set of vectors by VτV_{\tau}. Since VτV_{\tau} is a subset of the set of vertices of the convex hull of the unit cube [0,1]n[0,1]^{n} and the vectors −𝐞e-{\rm\mathbf{e}}_{e} for all e∈Ee\in E, every element of VτV_{\tau} is a vertex of ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} and ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} has no lattice points other than 𝟎\mathbf{0} and its vertices.

We now state two conjectures about the h∗h^{*}-vector of ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau}. For the example of Figure 1 we have h∗​(ℛτ)=(1,228,1614,1614,218,1)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}_{\tau})=(1,228,1614,1614,218,1) and h∗​(ℛτ∨)=(1,7,16,16,7,1)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau})=(1,7,16,16,7,1); in particular, ℛτ{\mathcal{R}}_{\tau} has 234 lattice points and ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} has 13 lattice points.

Conjecture 6.2.

We have h∗​(ℛτ∨)=h∗​(ℛτ∗∨)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau})=h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau^{\ast}}) (equivalently, Ehr⁡(ℛτ∨,t)=Ehr⁡(ℛτ∗∨,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau},t)={\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau^{\ast}},t)) for every preorder τ\tau.

Conjecture 6.3.

We have h∗​(ℛτ∨,t)=h∗​(ℛτ1∨,t)​h∗​(ℛτ2∨,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau},t)=h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau_{1}},t)\,h^{\ast}({\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau_{2}},t) if the preorder τ\tau is the ordinal sum of τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2}.

We are unable to explain the latter conjecture in terms of the structure of ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} since, in general, this polytope cannot be expressed as a free product.

Remark 6.4.

Curiously, the roots of the Ehrhart polynomial of ℛτ∨{\mathcal{R}}^{\vee}_{\tau} lie on the line Re(z)=−1/2\operatorname{Re}(z)=-1/2 for every preorder τ\tau of size at most 6. Assuming the validity of Conjecture 6.3, this property fails when τ\tau is the ordinal sum of two 5-element antichains.

7. Double Ehrhart theory

This section is concerned with the lattice point enumeration of the polytope 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s), introduced in Section 3.2.

Proposition 7.1.

There exists a polynomial 𝔼τ​(u,v)\mathbb{E}_{\tau}(u,v) of total degree nn such that 𝔼τ​(r,s)\mathbb{E}_{\tau}(r,s) is equal to the number of lattice points of 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) for all r,s∈ℕr,s\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

Since 𝒬τ​(r,s){\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}(r,s) can be expressed as the Minkowski sum of two nn-dimensional lattice polytopes with dilation factors rr and ss by Equation (8), the result follows from a general theorem of Bernstein–McMullen which defines multivariate Ehrhart polynomials; see, for instance, [Gru07, Theorem 19.4]. Alternatively, the explicit formula

(25) 𝔼τ​(r,s)=∑(ae)∈𝒢Gτ(s+a0a0)​∏e∈E(r+ae−1ae)\mathbb{E}_{\tau}(r,s)=\sum_{(a_{e})\in{\mathcal{G}}_{G_{\tau}}}\binom{s+a_{0}}{a_{0}}\prod_{e\in E}\binom{r+a_{e}-1}{a_{e}}

8. The MM-triangle

This section discusses another enumerative invariant of the poset of lattice points of a preorder polytope, namely the MM-triangle, and extends in this setting a conjecture of [Cha25b] on arbor polytopes. This conjecture provided much of the motivation behind the study of arbor polytopes; see [Cha25b, Section 1.1] for the global picture, which should extend verbatim to all preorder polytopes.

Let PP be a finite graded poset with rank function ρ:P→ℕ\rho:P\to\mathbb{N}. The MM-triangle of PP is defined by the formula

MP(x,y)=∑a,b∈P:a⪯bμP(a,b)xρ⁡(a)yρ⁡(b),M_{P}(x,y)=\sum_{a,b\,\in P:\,a\preceq b}\mu_{P}(a,b)x^{\rho(a)}y^{\rho(b)},

where μP\mu_{P} is the Möbius function of PP. The transmutation of a rational function f⁡(x,y)∈ℚ⁡(x,y)f(x,y)\in\mathbb{Q}(x,y) is defined as

f¯​(x,y)=f⁡(1−y1−x​y,1−x​y).\overline{f}(x,y)=f\left(\frac{1-y}{1-xy},1-xy\right).

We note that transmutation is an involution on ℚ⁡(x,y)\mathbb{Q}(x,y) and that M¯P​(x,y)∈ℤ⁡[x,y]\overline{M}_{P}(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y] for every graded poset PP. The following conjecture is stated implicitly for arbors in [Cha25b, Section 1.1].

Conjecture 8.1.

For every preorder τ\tau of size nn there exists a finite graded lattice LτL_{\tau} of rank nn such that 𝒵⁡(Pτ,t)=𝒵⁡(Lτ,t){\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},t)={\mathcal{Z}}(L_{\tau},t) and

(27) M¯Pτ​(x,y)=MLτ​(x,y).\overline{M}_{P_{\tau}}(x,y)=M_{L_{\tau}}(x,y).

In particular, the rank-generating polynomial of LτL_{\tau} is equal to h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t).

For example, if τ\tau is the chain preorder of size nn having nn vertices of cardinality 1 or one vertex of cardinality nn, then the role of LτL_{\tau} can be played by the noncrossing partition lattice of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n} and 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}, respectively; see Sections 7 and 8 of [Cha25b]. Thus, the poset PτP_{\tau} relates the combinatorics of the noncrossing partition lattice to that of the associahedron of corresponding type, the hh-polynomial of which is equal to h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t). Conjecture 8.1 predicts a similar relationship in a much more general context; we refer the reader to [Cha25b, Section 1.1] for an extensive discussion of this conjectural relationship in the setting of arbors.

The fact that Conjecture (8.1) implies that the rank-generating polynomial of LτL_{\tau} is equal to h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t) follows as in the special case of arbors; see [Cha25b, Proposition 5.1].

Our second conjecture states that the transmuted MM-triangle of PτP_{\tau} satisfies a certain duality.

Conjecture 8.2.

We have

(x​y)n​M¯Pτ​(1/x,1/y)=M¯Pτ​(y,x)(xy)^{n}\,\overline{M}_{P_{\tau}}(1/x,1/y)=\overline{M}_{P_{\tau}}(y,x)

for every preorder τ\tau of size nn.

Equivalently, MLτ​(x,y)=M(Lτ)∗​(x,y)M_{L_{\tau}}(x,y)=M_{(L_{\tau})^{\ast}}(x,y), where (Lτ)∗(L_{\tau})^{\ast} is the lattice dual to LτL_{\tau}.

Example 8.3.

Let us illustrate these concepts and conjectures with our running example. The MM-triangle can be displayed as a matrix of coefficients, with the constant term on the bottom left. For the running example from Figure 1 in dimension 5 with 92 elements and 18 maximal elements, this matrix is

−111−4375−60185−3584−8430−1043−572410−2414−551\begin{array}[]{rrrrrr}-1&11&-43&75&-60&18\\ 5&-35&84&-84&30&\\ -10&43&-57&24&&\\ 10&-24&14&&&\\ -5&5&&&&\\ 1&&&&&\end{array}

where the diagonal counts elements according to their sum of coordinates. The leftmost column comes from the unit cube contained in 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}. The transmutation of this MM-triangle is displayed by the matrix

−1860−7543−11160−174180−7711−75180−1393443−7734−11111\begin{array}[]{rrrrrr}-18&60&-75&43&-11&1\\ 60&-174&180&-77&11&\\ -75&180&-139&34&&\\ 43&-77&34&&&\\ -11&11&&&&\\ 1&&&&&\end{array}

where the diagonal is now the hh-vector. The identity claimed in Conjecture 8.2 is represented by the symmetry of the transmuted matrix in the main diagonal. Note that the number of maximal elements becomes, up to sign, the corner entry of the transmuted matrix.

9. Examples

The context of preorders allows for several interesting new examples of preorder polytopes, compared to the more restrictive setting of arbors. This section studies such examples in some detail. We let

Narn𝔸⁡(t)=∑i=0n1i+1​(ni)​(n+1i)​ti\operatorname{Nar}^{\mathbb{A}}_{n}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{1}{i+1}\binom{n}{i}\binom{n+1}{i}t^{i}

and

Narn𝔹⁡(t)=∑i=0n(ni)2​ti\operatorname{Nar}^{\mathbb{B}}_{n}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2}t^{i}

be the Narayana polynomials of type 𝔸n\mathbb{A}_{n} and 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n}, respectively.

9.1. Zig-zag posets

Given a positive integer nn, the zig-zag poset ZnZ_{n} is defined as the partial order on the set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\} with cover relations i≺i+1i\prec i+1 for all odd i∈{1,2,…,n−1}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n-1\} and i≻i+1i\succ i+1 for all even i∈{1,2,…,n−1}i\in\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}. Let us denote by 𝒬n{\mathcal{Q}}_{n} the preorder polytope and by hn​(t)h_{n}(t) the hh-polynomial associated to τ=Zn\tau=Z_{n}. The nnth Delannoy polynomial A008288, denoted by dn​(t)d_{n}(t), is defined by the recurrence

(28) dn​(t)=(1+t)​dn−1​(t)+t​dn−2​(t)d_{n}(t)=(1+t)d_{n-1}(t)+td_{n-2}(t)

for n≥2n\geq 2, with initial conditions d0​(t)=1d_{0}(t)=1 and d1​(t)=1+td_{1}(t)=1+t; we refer the reader to [WZC19] and the references given there for combinatorial interpretations and explicit formulas for these polynomials. The sum of the coefficients of dn​(t)d_{n}(t) satisfies the recurrence dn​(1)=2​dn−1​(1)+dn−2​(1)d_{n}(1)=2d_{n-1}(1)+d_{n-2}(1) for n≥2n\geq 2, where d0​(1)=1d_{0}(1)=1 and d1​(1)=2d_{1}(1)=2, which yields the Pell numbers A000129.

Proposition 9.1.

We have hn​(t)=dn​(t)h_{n}(t)=d_{n}(t) for every n≥1n\geq 1. In particular, the number of lattice points of 𝒬n{\mathcal{Q}}_{n} is equal to the Pell number dn​(1)d_{n}(1).

Proof.

Let n≥4n\geq 4 be even. The set of lattice points (a1,a2,…,an)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) of 𝒬n{\mathcal{Q}}_{n} can be expressed as the disjoint union of nonempty subsets by the following conditions:

  • •

    an=0a_{n}=0,

  • •

    an=1a_{n}=1,

  • •

    an=2a_{n}=2, which implies an−1=0a_{n-1}=0.

As one can easily verify, these sets are in one-to-one correspondence with the set of lattice points of 𝒬n−1{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1}, 𝒬n−1{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1} and 𝒬n−2{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-2}, respectively, so that

hn​(t)=(1+t)​hn−1​(t)+t​hn−2​(t).h_{n}(t)=(1+t)h_{n-1}(t)+th_{n-2}(t).

Similarly, the set of lattice points (a1,a2,…,an+1)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n+1}) of 𝒬n+1{\mathcal{Q}}_{n+1} can be expressed as the disjoint union of nonempty subsets by the following conditions:

  • •

    an+1=1a_{n+1}=1,

  • •

    an+1=0a_{n+1}=0 and an=0a_{n}=0,

  • •

    an+1=0a_{n+1}=0 and an=1a_{n}=1,

  • •

    an+1=0a_{n+1}=0 and an=2a_{n}=2,

  • •

    an+1=0a_{n+1}=0 and an=3a_{n}=3, which implies an−1=0a_{n-1}=0.

These sets are in one-to-one correspondence with the set of lattice points of 𝒬n{\mathcal{Q}}_{n}, 𝒬n−1{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1}, 𝒬n−1{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1}, 𝒬n−1{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-1} and 𝒬n−2{\mathcal{Q}}_{n-2}, respectively, so

hn+1​(t)=t​hn​(t)+(1+2​t)​hn−1​(t)+t​hn−2​(t)=(1+t)​hn​(t)+t​hn−1​(t).h_{n+1}(t)=th_{n}(t)+(1+2t)h_{n-1}(t)+th_{n-2}(t)=(1+t)h_{n}(t)+th_{n-1}(t).

Setting h0​(t)=1h_{0}(t)=1, and since h1​(t)=1+th_{1}(t)=1+t, h2​(t)=1+3​t+t2h_{2}(t)=1+3t+t^{2} and h3​(t)=1+5​t+5​t2+t3h_{3}(t)=1+5t+5t^{2}+t^{3}, we have shown that hn​(t)h_{n}(t) satisfies the recurrence (28) for n≥2n\geq 2 and the proof follows. ∎

The Delannoy polynomial dn​(t)d_{n}(t) is known to have all properties stated in Conjectures 5.1 - 5.3. The palindromicity of dn​(t)d_{n}(t) follows directly from (28); its γ\gamma-positivity and real-rootedness was shown in [WZC19]. The polynomial dn​(t)d_{n}(t) was shown to be equal to the hh-polynomial of a flag simplicial polytope (whose boundary complex is isomorphic to the independence complex of a planar ternary graph) in [BDHKY26]. We suspect that dn​(t)d_{n}(t) is also equal to the hh-polynomial of the nn-dimensional pellytope [BTT25] [HLRZ20, §4]; see [Alm22, Conjecture 6.1.36] for a related conjecture. This example is also related to the lattices of sashes [Law13, Law14].

9.2. Ordinal sums of antichains

For positive integers m,nm,n we will denote by τm,n\tau_{m,n} the set {1,2,…,m}⊔{1′,2′,…,n′}\{1,2,\dots,m\}\sqcup\{1^{\prime},2^{\prime},\dots,n^{\prime}\} partially ordered so that the cover relations are i≺j′i\prec j^{\prime} for all i,ji,j. Thus, τm,n\tau_{m,n} is the ordinal sum of an mm-element antichain and an nn-element antichain. Let us denote by 𝒬m,n{\mathcal{Q}}_{m,n} the preorder polytope and by hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t) the hh-polynomial associated to τm,n\tau_{m,n}.

Proposition 9.2.

The number of lattice points of 𝒬m,n{\mathcal{Q}}_{m,n} is equal to

∑k=0m∑ℓ=0n(k+ℓk)​(mk)​(nℓ)\sum_{k=0}^{m}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}\binom{k+\ell}{k}\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{\ell}

and

hm,n​(t)\displaystyle h_{m,n}(t) =∑k=0m∑ℓ=0n(k+ℓk)​(mk)​(nℓ)​tm−k+ℓ\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}\binom{k+\ell}{k}\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{\ell}t^{m-k+\ell}
=∑i≥0(mi)​(ni)​ti​(1+t)m+n−2​i\displaystyle=\sum_{i\geq 0}\binom{m}{i}\binom{n}{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{m+n-2i}

for all m,nm,n. In particular, hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t) is palindromic and γ\gamma-positive. Moreover, all roots of hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t) are real.

Proof.

Clearly, it suffices to prove the proposed formulas for hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t). By definition, the lattice points of 𝒬m,n{\mathcal{Q}}_{m,n} are the tuples (a1,a2,…,am,b1,b2,…,bn)∈ℕm+n(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{m},b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{m+n} such that ai∈{0,1}a_{i}\in\{0,1\} for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and

(29) bj1+bj2+⋯+bjr+a1+a2+⋯+am≤m+rb_{j_{1}}+b_{j_{2}}+\cdots+b_{j_{r}}+a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{m}\leq m+r

for all 1≤j1<j2<⋯<jr≤n1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\cdots<j_{r}\leq n. Suppose that we have ai=1a_{i}=1 for kk indices i∈{1,2,…,m}i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\} and bj≥1b_{j}\geq 1 for ℓ\ell indices j∈{1,2,…,n}j\in\{1,2,\dots,n\} and set cj=bj−1c_{j}=b_{j}-1 for such indices jj. By symmetry, we may assume that b1,b2,…,bℓ≥1b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{\ell}\geq 1. Then, the inequalities (29) become

cj1+cj2+⋯+cjr≤m−kc_{j_{1}}+c_{j_{2}}+\cdots+c_{j_{r}}\leq m-k

for 1≤j1<j2<⋯<jr≤ℓ1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\cdots<j_{r}\leq\ell and are thus equivalent to the single inequality

c1+c2+⋯+cℓ≤m−k.c_{1}+c_{2}+\cdots+c_{\ell}\leq m-k.

As a result, there are (mk)\binom{m}{k} ways to choose a1,a2,…,am∈{0,1}a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{m}\in\{0,1\} and for every such choice there are (nℓ)​(m−k+ℓℓ)\binom{n}{\ell}\binom{m-k+\ell}{\ell} ways to choose b1,b2,…,bnb_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n}. Therefore,

hm,n​(t)=∑k=0m∑ℓ=0n(m−k+ℓℓ)​(mk)​(nℓ)​tk+ℓ.h_{m,n}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}\binom{m-k+\ell}{\ell}\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{\ell}t^{k+\ell}.

This formula is equivalent to the first formula proposed for hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t). Since the right-hand side is equal to the rank-generating polynomial of the poset of shuffles of (1,2,…,m)(1,2,\dots,m) and (1′,2′,…,n′)(1^{\prime},2^{\prime},\dots,n^{\prime}) [Gre88], the second formula proposed for hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t) follows from [Gre88, Corollary 4.8].

Finally, we observe that ∑i≥0(mi)​(ni)​ti\sum_{i\geq 0}\binom{m}{i}\binom{n}{i}t^{i} is real-rooted as a Hadamard product of real-rooted polynomials [PS72, V 155]. By [Gal05, Remark 3.1.1], so is hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t). ∎

The enumerative combinatorics of the shuffle poset [Gre88] is closely related to that of the bubble lattice for the same parameters, introduced and studied in [MM22, MM24, MM25]. A shellable triangulation of a sphere with hh-polynomial equal to hm,n​(t)h_{m,n}(t) is the noncrossing bipartite complex of [MM25, Section 4]; see also [MM25, Remark 4.16].

4 6362 (1,40,410,1540,2380,1540,410,40,1)(1,40,410,1540,2380,1540,410,40,1)

The lattice path interpretation of the lattice points described (for all chain preorders) in [Ath25, Section 2] shows that the number of lattice points is given by sequence A066357. The generating function

1+x+6​x2+53​x3+554​x4+6362​x5+⋯1+x+6x^{2}+53x^{3}+554x^{4}+6362x^{5}+\cdots

of the number of lattice points is the inverse of

1−∑n≥112​n​(4​n−22​n−1)​xn=1−x−5​x2−42​x3−429​x4−4862​x5−⋯1-\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{1}{2n}\binom{4n-2}{2n-1}x^{n}=1-x-5x^{2}-42x^{3}-429x^{4}-4862x^{5}-\cdots

and the generating function

1+x+(t+4+t−1)​x2+(t2+12​t+27+12​t−1+t−2)​x3+⋯1+x+\left(t+4+t^{-1}\right)x^{2}+\left(t^{2}+12t+27+12t^{-1}+t^{-2}\right)x^{3}+\cdots

of the hh-polynomial is the inverse of 1−∑n≥1Nar2​n−2𝔸⁡(t)​t−n+1​xn1-\sum_{n\geq 1}\operatorname{Nar}^{\mathbb{A}}_{2n-2}(t)\,t^{-n+1}x^{n}.

9.5. Multiple chains

Let us consider the chain preorder τn,k\tau_{n,k} having nn vertices, each of cardinality kk. Experimental evidence suggests that

1+∑n≥1h⁡(τn,k,t2)​t−n​k​xn=exp⁡(∑n≥1Nark​n𝔹⁡(t2)​t−k​n​xnn).1+\sum_{n\geq 1}h(\tau_{n,k},t^{2})\,t^{-nk}x^{n}=\exp\left(\,\sum_{n\geq 1}\operatorname{Nar}^{\mathbb{B}}_{kn}(t^{2})\,t^{-kn}\,\frac{x^{n}}{n}\right).

When kk is even, one can replace tt by t1/2t^{1/2} and still get Laurent polynomials in tt. For k=2k=2 this gives a different interpretation of the hh-polynomial from that of Section 9.4; see A181145.

9.6. Comb posets

Let τn\tau_{n} be the poset defined recursively for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} as follows. The poset τ0\tau_{0} is empty and τn+1\tau_{n+1} is obtained from τn\tau_{n} by first taking the disjoint union with a poset with one element and then adding a new minimum element. For small values of nn, we have:

nn number of lattice points hh-vector
1 5 (1,3,1)(1,3,1)
2 33 (1,8,15,8,1)(1,8,15,8,1)
3 249 (1,15,61,95,61,15,1)(1,15,61,95,61,15,1)
4 2033 (1,24,166,484,683,484,166,24,1)(1,24,166,484,683,484,166,24,1)

which suggests that the number of lattice points of the associated preorder polytope is given by sequence A034015. The generating function

x+5​x2+33​x3+249​x4+2033​x5+⋯x+5x^{2}+33x^{3}+249x^{4}+2033x^{5}+\cdots

of this sequence is the compositional inverse of

∑n≥1(−1)n−1​(1+2n​(n−1))​xn=x−5​x2+17​x3−49​x4+129​x5−⋯,\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n-1}\left(1+2^{n}(n-1)\right)x^{n}=x-5x^{2}+17x^{3}-49x^{4}+129x^{5}-\cdots,

see A000337. This leads us to suspect that the generating function of the hh-polynomial

x+(t+3+t−1)​x2+(t2+8​t+15+8​t−1+t−2)​x3+⋯x+\left(t+3+t^{-1}\right)x^{2}+\left(t^{2}+8t+15+8t^{-1}+t^{-2}\right)x^{3}+\cdots

is the compositional inverse of

∑n≥1(−1)n−1​(1+(1+t)n​(1+t+⋯+tn−2)​t−n+1)​xn.\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n-1}\left(1+{(1+t)}^{n}(1+t+\cdots+t^{n-2})\,t^{-n+1}\right)x^{n}.
